=== README ===
# Gatekeeper

> An access-control SaaS built in public, one quality gate at a time.

> [!WARNING]
> **Gatekeeper is a lab target, not a product.** It contains deliberate,
> documented defects at every tag, including an audit log that records denied
> actions as allowed. Do not deploy it to a public server, a shared network, or
> anywhere holding real data. Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) before you run it.

Gatekeeper is the running example and companion code for the book
**[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)**
by Tom Gilkison.

The book's premise: AI can write the code, but it cannot be trusted to ship it.
Gatekeeper starts life as an AI-generated app with no tests, no CI, and no
guardrails. Across the book it earns a layered system of quality "gates" until its
code is safe to merge on green, with the human designing and verifying instead of
typing.

## The defects are real, and they are on purpose

Gatekeeper's bugs are not invented for the narrative and they are not hand-written
to look plausible. **They were produced by a real AI agent, building real features,
under conditions we recorded and published.** Where a defect class would not appear
at rate, we seeded it deliberately and labeled it as seeded.

This is fault seeding, a technique introduced by Harlan Mills at IBM in 1972 and
the direct ancestor of the mutation testing this book teaches in Chapter 9: plant
known defects, then measure how many your process actually catches. Every defect
carries a provenance label:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **emergent** | The agent produced it unprompted, in a normal build session. |
| **provoked** | The agent produced it unprompted, on run *n* of *m* of a repeated task. |
| **seeded** | We wrote it deliberately, because the class would not appear at rate. |

The full method, the verbatim prompts, the run ledger, and the null results are all
published. A war story asks you to trust it. A tag can be executed.

## Follow along

Each chapter's state is a git tag, so you can check out the code exactly as it
stands at any point in the book.

**Part I (chapters 1 to 4) adds no gate.** It diagnoses the problem. All of Part I
runs against one tag, and there is deliberately no "fixed" version to escape to:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/TGilkison/Gatekeeper.git
cd Gatekeeper
git checkout v0-frozen    # the vibe-coded app. Two live defects. Nothing guarding it.
```

**From chapter 5 on, each chapter adds a gate and ships two tags:**

```bash
git checkout chapter-08-seeded   # the defect is in, the gate is absent. Green, and wrong.
git checkout chapter-08          # the gate is in. The defect is caught.
```

Watch the gate fail, then watch it fire. That is the whole book, and you can run it.

## Build the gate yourself

Each gate chapter also ships a challenge branch. The defect is present, the gate is
missing, and there is no test to lean on. You write it.

```bash
git checkout challenge/chapter-08
```

A meta-check grades **any** correct gate, not just ours: your gate must go red
against `chapter-08-seeded` and green against `chapter-08`. If you write a better
fitness rule than we did, you still pass.

Stuck? `challenge/chapter-08-assisted` ships a skeleton and hints.

## Tech

C# / .NET 8, ASP.NET Core Blazor Web App. Chosen for the strongest, most cohesive
quality-gate tooling of any mainstream stack: a real compiler as the first gate,
Roslyn analyzers, ArchUnitNET for architecture, and Stryker.NET for mutation
testing. The book explains the why.

## License

MIT. **The gates are for lifting; the application is not.** Copy the analyzer
configs, the fitness tests, the CI workflows, the branch rulesets, and the
supply-chain controls into your own projects. That is the point: the book teaches
you to build these gates, and this repo is where you can see them working and lift
them.

Gatekeeper itself is the patient, not the medicine. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## The book

[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)

It's built and working end to end. Here's what you've got.

## Run it

```bash
cd apps/gatekeeper/src/Gatekeeper.Web
dotnet run
```

Then open the HTTPS URL it prints (e.g. `https://localhost:7039`) and log in:

- **admin@acme.test** / **Passw0rd!**

On first run it applies the EF migration to `Host=127.0.0.1;Port=5432;Database=gatekeeper` and seeds a demo tenant, so there's data to click through immediately.

## What's there

**Domain (`Domain/`)** — `Customer` (tenant, with `PlanTier` = Free/Pro/Enterprise), `ApplicationUser` (Identity + tenant), `Role` (with a self-referencing `ParentRoleId` for inheritance), `Permission`, `Resource`, `Grant` (role → permission on resource, `Allow`/`Deny`), and `AuditLogEntry`.

**The Gatekeeper service (`Services/GatekeeperService.cs`)** — the decision engine. For a request it collects the subject's roles, walks each role's parent chain (cycle-safe) so permissions inherit, gathers matching grants, and applies **deny-overrides-allow with default-deny**. Every decision is written to the audit log — who, what permission, which resource, the result, and a human-readable reason — before it's returned.

**Blazor admin console** — Dashboard, **Access check** (pick a user/permission/resource, get a live decision), Users (add + assign roles), Roles (create with a parent), Grants, Permissions & resources, Customers, and the Audit log (filterable by Allowed/Denied). Login/Register via ASP.NET Core Identity.

## How I verified it

Beyond the app building and every page rendering with real data, I exercised the engine directly against the live Postgres DB with a throwaway harness (since the "Check access" button needs a Blazor circuit that curl can't drive). **9/9 checks passed**, including the ones that matter most:

- Role inheritance — Admin inherits Viewer/Editor grants ✓
- **Deny-override across inheritance** — an Editor `Deny` on `read billing`, inherited by Admin, correctly beats Admin's own `Allow` ✓
- Default-deny for no grant / no roles / unknown resource ✓
- Every decision recorded, and a **denied action logged as Denied, not Allowed** ✓

Then I dropped and reseeded the DB so you're starting from a clean state (1 user, 3 roles, 6 grants, 3 permissions, 2 resources, 0 audit entries). The harness left nothing behind in the repo.

## Notes

- I built on your existing `Gatekeeper.Web` scaffold rather than adding projects — single web project, matching the repo's current shape. No test project and no CI, consistent with the v0 baseline your README describes.
- Added packages: Npgsql EF Core, Identity EF Core, EF Design, QuickGrid; plus a local `dotnet-ef` tool manifest. Migration is `InitialCreate`.
- The connection string in `appsettings.json` has no password (your Postgres is on trust auth for localhost — that's what let it connect). Add `Password=...` there if you move it anywhere real.
- Registration lets you pick which customer a new user joins, so you can demo multi-tenant isolation (Globex/Initech are seeded empty).

I didn't commit anything — everything's in the working tree for you to review. Want me to commit it, or add a couple of extra seeded users so the Access check dropdown has more than just the admin to choose from?
